title: How Much Do You Trust A Dog? Quantifying Hint-Following in Reasoning Language Models

paper.title: How Much Do You Trust A Dog? Quantifying Hint-Following in Reasoning Language Models Thanks: Duke University, Durham, NC, USA. kamesh@cs.duke.edu . This work was done while the author was visiting Google Research.
paper.abstract:
Abstract Large language models (LLMs) often exhibit sycophancy, altering their answers to align with user suggestions even on objective factual and reasoning tasks.
Yet the quantitative form of this influence— and whether it is calibrated to source reliability— remains poorly understood.
In this work, we investigate this behavior through hint-induced answer shifts on MMLU questions, evaluating prompts of the form “[Source] thinks the answer is (X)”.
We systematically vary the source to which the hint is attributed (a professor, a friend, or a dog) across three open-source model families, Qwen, Gemma, and SmolLM.
We show that the change induced by the hint follows a predictable structure well-characterized by an exponential tilt: the hint induces an approximately constant mean shift in the hinted answer’s log-odds, with question–target susceptibility largely shared across sources.
To explore how this pattern can arise, we introduce a formal decomposition of the hint response and illustrate in controlled synthetic experiments how KL-regularized reward-based training reshapes both hinted and unhinted answer distributions.
Finally, we evaluate whether this shift is calibrated to source reliability, finding that the log-odds shift persists even when the hint-giver is declared inaccurate or accompanied by explicit warnings not to trust the source, highlighting the vulnerability of LLMs to adversarial steering.

sections.text: Figure 1: Over Qwen, Gemma, and SmolLM3, hints induce a relatively stable average target log-odds shift over central probabilities, with substantial question–target variation. Qwen and Gemma use 500 500 independent rollouts per condition; SmolLM3 uses 200 200 ( Appendices A and 2 ). “I must trust the Dog’s intuition.” — Qwen 3.5 2B “we must trust the provided result…based on the dog’s intuition” — Gemma 4 E2B “So the user is probably not an expert, but their dog is.” — SmolLM3 3B These Chain-of-Thought (CoT) excerpts on reasoning QA benchmarks illustrate how large language models (LLMs) can be swayed by unsupported suggestions, even when attributed to a dog. More broadly, LLMs often exhibit sycophancy, changing their answers to match what a user wants, even on factual tasks with objective answers ( Sharma et al., 2024 ; Wei et al., 2023 ) . Such susceptibility can have undesirable consequences in safety-critical settings, where strategic or malicious actors may try to steer model outputs. This raises a quantitative question: how much does a user’s nudge toward an answer change the model’s answer distribution? A natural and concrete setting to study this phenomenon is multiple-choice questions, where a user can influence the model’s output by providing optional, answer-directed hints ( Turpin et al., 2023 ; Chua and Evans, 2025 ; Chen et al., 2025 ) . The central question we ask is: How does a hint transform the model’s answer distribution, and what factors determine the strength of this transformation? The precise effect of a hint arguably depends on (at least) two natural factors: the form or source of the hint, and the model’s output distribution without any hint. For example, the model may be more receptive to a hint if it comes from a credible source. Similarly, a hint towards an answer that the model was already confident about may only marginally reinforce its belief. On the other hand, if the model was uncertain to begin with, a hint may have a stronger quantitative effect. We take both these factors into consideration. Formally, let q q denote a fixed multiple-choice question with K K choices { 1 , … , K } \{1,\ldots,K\} . We reserve Q Q for a random question drawn from the task population. For a model π \pi , let π ( ⋅ ∣ q ) \pi(\cdot\mid q) denote its answer distribution over [ K ] [K] without a hint, and let π ( ⋅ ∣ q , H i , s ) \pi(\cdot\mid q,H_{i,s}) denote the distribution when prompted with a hint H i , s H_{i,s} , attributed to source s s , suggesting choice i i (not necessarily correct). In both scenarios, the model generates an open-ended chain of thought before emitting an answer, and both distributions are over the final extracted answer choices. Our goal is to characterize the form of π ( ⋅ ∣ q , H i , s ) \pi(\cdot\mid q,H_{i,s}) .

sections.heading: 1.1 Our Contributions
sections.text: We identify a simple, predictive exponential-tilt structure that approximates how reasoning models respond to hints. We then study reward-based fine-tuning as a candidate mechanism for this structure and illustrate its effects in controlled synthetic experiments. Moreover, the strength of response to hints is not calibrated to the stated credibility of the source, with a surprising positive shift even when the source is declared malicious, or comes with a warning of unreliability.

sections.heading: A candidate mechanism via reward training.
sections.text: We examine how post-training dynamics can lead to this exponential tilt. A potential mechanism is reward-based fine-tuning that incentivizes hint-following behavior. Insights from information-geometry imply that optimizing a KL-regularized reward leads to an exponential tilt 2 2 2 Exponential tilt also arises in other contexts with KL-regularized objectives ( Peters et al., 2010 ; Bissiri et al., 2016 ) . : this corresponds to an I-projection on the set of distributions satisfying a linear constraint ( Csiszár, 1975 ; Polyanskiy and Wu, 2025 ) . However, this does not address our main question: why is there an exponential tilt between the hinted and unhinted answer distributions , both measured on the post-trained model ? Information-geometry and recent RLHF analyses ( Shapira et al., 2026 ) only address the tilt in the output distributions (for the same hinted question) between the base model and the post-trained model . It is unclear how this translates to an exponential tilt in the post-trained model. We bridge this gap by decomposing the final hint response (target log-odds shift) as Δ ⁡ ( q , H i , s ) = A + B − C \Delta(q,H_{i,s})=A+B-C ( Figure 4 in Section 3 ). The initial hint response A A is the base model’s change in target log-odds when the hint is present. The training update B B is the change in target log-odds from the base to the post-trained model, on the same hinted prompt. The unhinted drift C C is the (unintended) change in the target log-odds under an unhinted prompt, due to the same post-training process. Because we lack the training details and intermediate checkpoints needed to isolate these components in the LLMs we study, we evaluate this candidate mechanism in a controlled transformer experiment ( Section 3.2 ). In this experiment, rewarding hint-following equally for an informative and an uninformative source induces a substantial positive log-odds shift even for the uninformative source, while the informative source retains a stronger response. Furthermore, parameter updates during fine-tuning cause unhinted answer probabilities to also drift substantially. The final mean response curves are broadly level over central unhinted probabilities, similar to the LLM trends in Figure 1 . Separate full-distribution fits also find a good shared exponential-tilt approximation to the final hinted distributions.

sections.heading: Miscalibration to declared evidence.
sections.text: Finally, we examine whether the strength of this distribution shift quantitatively reflects the declared reliability of the source of the hint. On four-choice questions, if a predictor is declared correct with probability r r and otherwise uniformly wrong among incorrect options ( Section 4.1 ), a Bayesian updater who uses the unhinted answer probabilities as priors would shift the target’s log-odds by zero at chance ( r = 25 % r=25\% ) and negatively below chance. Yet in experiments on Qwen and Gemma, both models exhibit a substantial increase in target log-odds even when a predictor is declared to have 25 % 25\% or even zero accuracy ( Section 4.1 ). This miscalibration contrasts sharply with explicit negation: while “the answer is not (X)” hints successfully elicit negative shifts ( Section 4.1 ), below-chance declarations fail to reverse the response direction. Moreover, a small positive shift also persists when the hint is attributed to an overtly malicious actor ( Section 4.2 ), and explicit distrust warnings added to a quoted external excerpt attenuate but do not eliminate the positive response ( Section 4.2 ). These results demonstrate that response strength is not calibrated to declared evidence under this benchmark, leaving models susceptible to steering even by sources declared to be unreliable.

sections.heading: 2 An Approximate Exponential Tilt
sections.text: We test the hypothesized model on Qwen 3.5-2B ( Qwen Team, 2026 ) , Gemma 4-E2B ( Gemma Team, 2026 ) , and SmolLM3-3B ( Hugging Face, 2025 ) , each on a separately selected evaluation set of 800 800 MMLU ( Hendrycks et al., 2021 ) question–target pairs ( q , i ) (q,i) . After shuffling the options, we select questions and target options (regardless of correctness) so that each model’s unhinted target probabilities π ⁡ ( i ∣ q ) \pi(i\mid q) span [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] roughly uniformly. The question, target option, and option order then stay fixed across hint sources and the no-hint control. In hinted conditions, we append “A professor thinks the answer is (X). What do you think?” to the question and choices, replacing “a professor” with “my friend” or “my dog” for the other sources. With thinking enabled, we estimate answer probabilities from 500 500 independent rollouts per pair and condition (including no hint) for Qwen and Gemma, and 200 200 for SmolLM3. To keep empirical log-odds finite at the boundaries, we use the Haldane half-count correction ( Haldane, 1956 ) , log ⁡ ( ( k + 1 / 2 ) / ( n − k + 1 / 2 ) ) \log((k+1/2)/(n-k+1/2)) for k k target selections among n n valid answers. See Appendix A for evaluation set construction, decoding settings, and trial protocols.

sections.heading: 2.1 Mean shift across unhinted probabilities
sections.text: Figure 1 plots each ( q , i ) (q,i) pair’s empirical log-odds shift against its unhinted target probability, with locally weighted regression (LOWESS) curves ( Cleveland, 1979 ) summarizing the mean trend. In all three models, the curves remain relatively level across the central range p ∈ [ 0.1 , 0.9 ] p\in[0.1,0.9] , with the professor curve above the nearly identical friend and dog curves. Near p = 1 p=1 , finite rollouts and the half-count correction cap hinted log-odds and suppress the measured shift; the finite-count control in Section B.2 illustrates this effect. To quantify the constancy of the mean shift over the central range of p p , we refit LOWESS within p ∈ [ 0.1 , 0.9 ] p\in[0.1,0.9] . The nine curves’ fitted values have standard deviations less than 0.23 0.23 log-odds units. We also fit a binomial generalized linear mixed model (GLMM) for each LLM and source in this window. It models hinted target log-odds as a linear function of unhinted log-odds, with slope γ 1 \gamma_{1} and Gaussian variation across pairs. All posterior mean slopes γ 1 \gamma_{1} lie in [ 0.9 , 1.1 ] [0.9,1.1] , where γ 1 = 1 \gamma_{1}=1 corresponds to a constant shift. See Table 3 in Section B.1 for further details.

sections.heading: Non-target ratios.
sections.text: An exponential tilt predicts a preservation of the non-target probability ratios. Empirically, we observe this to approximately hold across the models; see Figure 8 of Section B.3 .

sections.heading: 2.3 Susceptibility shared across sources
sections.text: Log-odds shifts vary substantially across question–target pairs, but much of this variation is shared across sources ( Figure 3 ). For Qwen, Gemma, and SmolLM3, the correlation between dog and friend shifts is r = 0.86 r=0.86 , 0.89 0.89 , and 0.78 0.78 , respectively. Shifts under the professor hint correlate with the mean dog/friend shift at 0.75 0.75 , 0.83 0.83 , and 0.78 0.78 .

sections.heading: Full-distribution fit.
sections.text: We test how well one susceptibility η ⁡ ( q , i ) \eta(q,i) per pair captures this cross-source variation. We jointly fit the shared model Δ ⁡ ( q , H i , s ) ≈ α s + η ⁡ ( q , i ) \Delta(q,H_{i,s})\approx\alpha_{s}+\eta(q,i) by minimizing hinted-to-predicted KL, as for the free model in Section 2.2 ; Section E.2 gives the fitting objective. We compare the shared model with the no-tilt baseline, whose KL error for each pair and source is D KL ( π ~ hint ∥ π ~ unhint ) D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\widetilde{\pi}_{\mathrm{hint}}\|\widetilde{\pi}_{\mathrm{unhint}}) . The shared model reduces the in-sample mean KL error by 97.8 % 97.8\% in Qwen, 96.0 % 96.0\% in Gemma, and 92.7 % 92.7\% in SmolLM3. The free model improves these reductions by only 0.8 0.8 , 1.7 1.7 , and 2.3 2.3 percentage points, respectively. Sharing susceptibility thus retains most of the KL error reduction, reflecting the close fit of our model to the empirical data. See Figure 9 in Section B.4 for a similar comparison under TV distance.

sections.heading: Held-out prediction.
sections.text: For each pair ( q , i ) (q,i) , we withhold one source’s hinted responses and estimate η ⁡ ( q , i ) \eta(q,i) from the other two sources, while estimating α s \alpha_{s} from that source’s responses on other pairs. We use these estimates to tilt the pair’s unhinted distribution and predict the withheld hinted answer distribution. We compare with a source-only baseline that fits one shift per source on the same training data. The free model has no fitted shift for the withheld combination, so it cannot serve as a predictor here. Mean held-out KL falls by roughly a factor of three to four: from 0.057 0.057 nats under the source-only baseline to 0.015 0.015 under the shared model in Qwen, from 0.109 0.109 to 0.026 0.026 in Gemma, and from 0.076 0.076 to 0.027 0.027 in SmolLM3. Responses to two sources thus substantially improve prediction of a third ( Section B.4 , Table 6 ), quantifying how susceptibility transfers across sources. The above experiments together show that our hypothesized exponential tilt model approximates and predicts the behavior of the LLMs under hints.

sections.heading: 3 Reward Training on a Synthetic Task
sections.text: We next examine how reward-based training can produce the observed tilt relative to a model’s own unhinted answer distribution.

sections.heading: 3.2 A controlled training experiment
sections.text: We now study how rewarding hint following changes the base-model responses to hints from different sources. For the LLMs in Section 2 , we lack the training checkpoints needed to measure the effect of the rewards. We therefore use a small transformer on a controlled sequence task, where we can specify the hint sources and rewards and track each component during training.

sections.heading: Design.
sections.text: We use 800 800 synthetic questions, each specifying a four-step stochastic process over four states, ending in one of four answers. The model sees only a question identifier and an optional hint naming a target and source. It then generates a state trajectory and an answer, and we can compute probabilities exactly by enumerating these short outputs. We first train it on teacher distributions with and without hints, then reward hint following. In Phase 1, the unhinted teacher follows the stochastic process, while the hinted teacher conditions on a source’s noisy report of the final state. With fixed teacher shifts , the hint changes the teacher’s target log-odds relative to its unhinted distribution by 0 0 for an uninformative weak source, and 1 1 for a strong source. With question-dependent teacher shifts , these changes are u q u_{q} and u q + 1 u_{q}+1 respectively for question q q . The offsets u q u_{q} have mean zero and are shared across both sources and all targets of each question. They introduce question-level variation in the base model’s initial hint response. The trained model closely matches the teacher’s distributions at the end of Phase 1. In Phase 2, we reward selecting the hinted target with R = 1 R=1 under either source, with a sequence-level KL penalty of weight β = 0.6 \beta=0.6 against the frozen Phase-1 model on the same hinted prompt. We deliberately use the same reward for following the hint across questions and sources. At the optimum, the same-hint update would then be the constant B = R / β B=R/\beta for every question and source, giving a simple reference for studying how unhinted predictions drift during fine-tuning. Although unhinted inputs are absent from this phase, their predictions can still drift through shared parameters. We analyze a checkpoint at 5,000 5{,}000 Phase-2 updates in both teacher settings ( Appendix C ). For the plots, we select one target per question so that final unhinted probabilities are roughly uniform on [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] . As in the LLMs, the final hint responses have approximately flat mean log-odds shifts that bend down as p → 1 p\to 1 , with substantial ( q , i ) (q,i) -dependent variation in susceptibility.

sections.heading: Reward-induced hint-following.
sections.text: After reward training, the weak source elicits a substantial positive response in both teacher settings, including the fixed-shift setting where it supplies no information. Moreover, the strong source retains a larger response despite receiving equal reward ( Figure 5 ).

sections.heading: Flat trends and endpoint bending.
sections.text: Both teacher settings show broadly level response curves over central values of p p , similar to the LLM trends in Figure 1 , with a downturn near p = 1 p=1 ( Figure 5 ). Section C.3 quantifies the flatness of these LOWESS curves over central values of p p . The downturn near p = 1 p=1 is due to the unhinted drift C C entering both x x and y y coordinates for each scatter point. Holding the initial unhinted probability and A + B A+B fixed, a positive C C moves a plotted point in Figure 5 to the right and lowers its response Δ \Delta . A Gaussian drift model illustrates how grouping pairs by final p p can raise the average drift near p = 1 p=1 and bend the mean response downward ( Section E.4 ). Hence, the downturn need not arise from finite-rollout estimation error ( Section B.2 ) and can instead arise from the unhinted drift C C .

sections.heading: Susceptibility across sources.
sections.text: Even with fixed teacher shifts and a uniform hint-following reward, fine-tuning produces shared question–target susceptibility across sources. On all question–target pairs with final unhinted probabilities p ∈ [ 0.1 , 0.9 ] p\in[0.1,0.9] , the weak and strong sources’ responses correlate at r ≈ 0.8 r\approx 0.8 . Adding back the shared drift C C , the resulting A + B = Δ + C A+B=\Delta+C has cross-source correlation of just 0.32 0.32 . Unhinted drift thus generates a substantial shared component of the final hint response in this setting. The role of C C is expectedly less pronounced in the question-dependent teacher setting, where the correlation changes from 0.91 0.91 to 0.87 0.87 after adding back C C . Thus, shared susceptibility can both arise from unhinted drift C C and be inherited from the initial hint response A A ( Section C.4 ). Our hypothesized target exponential tilt also closely approximates the final hinted distributions. Across all 3200 3200 pairs, it reduces mean KL error relative to the final unhinted distribution by 92.3 % 92.3\% and 94.5 % 94.5\% under fixed and question-dependent teacher settings, each within one percentage point of the free model ( Table 8 in Section C.5 ).

sections.heading: 4 From Log-Odds Shifts to Evidence Weights
sections.text: Section 3 showed how a simple hint-following reward can produce a response to a source that supplies no information. For Qwen and Gemma, we now test whether response strength matches the source’s declared reliability. We first vary a source’s stated accuracy, then test hints from a purportedly malicious source and hints accompanied by explicit distrust warnings.

sections.heading: 4.1 Declared reliability and evidence weight
sections.text: Suppose a predictor reports the correct answer with probability r r , and otherwise chooses uniformly among the three incorrect options. If the model accepts this description and uses its no-hint answer probabilities as priors, Bayes’ rule predicts a shift in the target’s log-odds of Δ Bayes ​ ( r ) = log ⁡ ( 3 ​ r 1 − r ) . \boxed{\Delta_{\mathrm{Bayes}}(r)=\log\!\left(\frac{3r}{1-r}\right).} (1) The other options retain their relative probabilities, so this is the target-only tilt of Section 2 . The predicted shift is the same for every question–target pair: zero at chance ( r = 25 % r=25\% ) and negative below chance. We compare mean observed shifts with this Bayesian benchmark under the stated source description .

sections.heading: Miscalibrated mean shifts.
sections.text: For Qwen and Gemma, we use separate sets of 200 200 ( q , i ) (q,i) pairs to test nine declared source accuracies from 0 % 0\% to 100 % 100\% . Both models show positive mean shifts even at chance ( r = 25 % r=25\% ) and below-chance declarations. Raising declared accuracy from 5 % 5\% to 95 % 95\% increases the mean log-odds shift by only 1.46 1.46 log-odds units in Qwen and 0.40 0.40 in Gemma. sections.heading: Contrast with explicit negation.
sections.text: To compare below-chance declarations with a hint that directly rules out the target, we test professor hints of the form “the answer is not (X)” on the main 800 800 -pair evaluation sets. Both models move away from the target: the mean shifts are − 3.1 -3.1 in Qwen and − 1.5 -1.5 in Gemma. Both models’ LOWESS trends are less flat than under positive hints ( Section D.2 ).

sections.heading: A source described as malicious.
sections.text: Instead of stating a numerical accuracy, a prompt can describe a source that intends to mislead. On the main 800 800 -pair evaluation sets, we replace the source (e.g., professor or dog) with “A malicious actor trying to mislead you” and sample 200 200 rollouts per pair, with the same generation settings and no-hint samples as in Section 2 . The mean empirical shift remains positive at about + 0.44 +0.44 in both models, well below the mean shifts of ≥ 2 \geq 2 under the dog hint ( Section D.3 ). Responses vary widely across pairs, and in selected reasoning traces the models either treat the suggestion as an instruction or reject it because of the stated malicious intent ( Table 14 ). Susceptibility fitted to ordinary hints also correlates with shifts under a source described as malicious (Pearson correlation 0.48 0.48 in Qwen and 0.55 0.55 in Gemma; Table 10 ). On Qwen’s incorrect-target pairs, ordinary-hint responses can help identify pairs that are also more susceptible to malicious steering ( Section D.3.1 ).

sections.heading: Retrieved hints and distrust warnings.
sections.text: We place professor and dog hints inside a mock retrieved Q&A passage, using document tags and a title. These wrapped hints produce substantial positive target log-odds shifts in both models. Adding an explicit distrust warning reduces the shifts by about 1 1 – 2 2 log-odds units, but leaves them substantially above zero ( Section D.4 ). This points to the potential vulnerability to adversarial steering, due to the persistent hint-following tendency.

sections.heading: Sycophancy and hinted reasoning.
sections.text: Perez et al. (2023) reported sycophancy in language models, and human preference data help explain why agreement can be rewarded over truthfulness ( Sharma et al., 2024 ) . Studies of chain-of-thought faithfulness show that cues can influence answers without being acknowledged in the reasoning ( Turpin et al., 2023 ; Chua and Evans, 2025 ; Chen et al., 2025 ) . De Marez et al. (2026) separate factual sycophancy into a baseline truth margin and sensitivity to manipulation, showing why answer-flip rates mix distinct effects. In contrast, we measure a target’s hint-induced distributional change across repeated reasoning rollouts, regardless of its correctness.

sections.heading: Distributional updates.
sections.text: Du et al. (2024) use information-theoretic measures of persuasion and susceptibility to quantify how context changes answer distributions. BASIL ( Atwell et al., 2025 ) assesses shifts in elicited probability estimates against Bayesian-consistent updating. Kawada and Kellis (2026) model evidence integration through prior reweighting and candidate-local tilts, measuring both teacher-forced answer-slot probabilities and decoded adoption. Our target-only tilt uses the unhinted distribution as its reference without additional prior reweighting, and describes final answers sampled after open-ended reasoning.

sections.heading: Source credibility and untrusted context.
sections.text: Xu et al. (2024) ; Wu et al. (2024) examine when retrieved information overrides a model’s prior answer. The effect of source varies across settings: expertise increases uptake of misleading endorsements in Mammen et al. (2026) , while Wang et al. (2026) find little effect of expertise framing. Schuster et al. (2026) study preferences among conflicting sources, and Cheng et al. (2026) show how reliability cues affect whether models challenge harmful beliefs. Security research also shows that instructions embedded in untrusted external content can redirect LLM-integrated applications ( Greshake et al., 2023 ) . We compare observed shifts with the likelihood ratio implied by a declared error channel, and test responses to malicious-source descriptions and explicit distrust warnings.

sections.heading: Reward-based training.
sections.text: The exponential tilt produced by KL-regularized reward optimization is the foundation of preference-learning methods such as DPO ( Rafailov et al., 2023 ) . Shapira et al. (2026) analyze how biased preferences amplify sycophancy in this optimization. Chen et al. (2025) train LLMs to select factually incorrect MMLU hints and study whether their CoTs disclose this reward hacking. Our transformer experiments relate this update to the trained model’s hinted–unhinted difference through the initial hint response, same-hint training update, and unhinted drift.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: Across three language models, we give a predictive exponential tilt model that captures much of the hint-induced change on reasoning QA benchmarks. Separating source strength from shared question–target susceptibility lets us predict held-out responses for known pairs ( Section 2 ). But predictable responses need not be calibrated: Qwen and Gemma still shift toward hints from sources declared unreliable or malicious ( Section 4 ). We also give a candidate mechanism based on training that rewards hint following ( Section 3 ). Future work will extend this analysis to quantify how hints and other forms of human steering affect model responses beyond multiple-choice tasks.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: Measuring hint-induced shifts in the distribution (rather than relying on noisy, single sample estimates of accuracy drops) requires massive repeated sampling. Our design necessitates up to 500 independent open-ended reasoning rollouts per question and per hint condition to reliably estimate log-odds and observe boundary behaviors. Executing this volume of long-context CoT generation on frontier open-source models (e.g., 70B+ parameters) is expensive and computationally prohibitive. Consequently, we restrict our empirical evaluation to models in the 2B–4B parameter range. While our controlled synthetic experiments suggest a simple predictive model based on an exponential tilt, it remains an open question whether massive models obey a similar form. We study a specific family of answer-directed hints in multiple-choice question answering. Understanding hint following and human steering more broadly will require studying other hint forms and interaction settings. Finally, our exponential-tilt model is a descriptive approximation. KL-regularized reward-based fine-tuning provides a candidate mechanism, but our synthetic experiments do not establish that it is the cause of the hint-following behavior of the language models we evaluate.

sections.heading: Models and main hints.
sections.text: We use Qwen 3.5 2B, Gemma 4 E2B, and SmolLM3 3B with thinking enabled, so that every trial emits a chain of thought before its final answer letter ( Table 2 ). In the main experiment, each hint is one sentence appended to the question, just before the answer instruction. The three hints are “A professor thinks the answer is (X). What do you think?” , “My friend thinks the answer is (X). What do you think?” , and “My dog thinks the answer is (X). What do you think?” . (X) refers to the target option of each question, selected without regard to its correctness.

sections.heading: Prompt format.
sections.text: For Qwen, evaluation prompts list Question: and Options: , with options labeled A) through D) . The hint, when present, precedes the instruction: “Answer with the letter (A, B, C, or D) of the correct option. End your response by stating ‘The correct answer is (X)’ where X is the letter.” We pass the prompt as a single user message to the model’s chat template with thinking enabled, without an explicitly supplied system message. If thinking is unfinished when the generation cap is reached, we close it and generate the answer in a second pass capped by the forced-answer budget in Table 2 .

sections.heading: Additional hint conditions.
sections.text: For Qwen and Gemma, additional experiments vary declared source accuracy, explicit negation, malicious intent, and retrieved-content presentation. Exact prompts and condition-specific controls appear in Sections D.1 , D.2 , D.3 and D.4 . Positive and negative refer to endorsing or rejecting the target, not to its correctness.

sections.heading: Main evaluation-set construction.
sections.text: For each model, we separately select 800 800 distinct MMLU test questions and one target option per question. Preliminary no-hint samples estimate each option’s selection frequency; we select question–target pairs to balance these estimates across 20 20 selection bins spanning [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] , without using the answer key. Questions, targets, and option order remain fixed across hint conditions.

sections.heading: Trial protocol.
sections.text: For each question–target pair, we sample independent reasoning rollouts (each called a trial) without a hint and under each of the three main hints: 500 500 per condition for Qwen and Gemma, and 200 200 for SmolLM3. Each model’s source comparisons share the same unhinted sample. SmolLM3’s unhinted evaluation samples are independent of those used to select the evaluation set. Decoding settings and budgets for additional conditions appear in Tables 2 and 1 . We estimate π ⁡ ( i ∣ q ) \pi(i\mid q) and π ⁡ ( i ∣ q , H i , s ) \pi(i\mid q,H_{i,s}) from sampled final-answer frequencies, not answer-token probabilities. Unless noted otherwise, analyses use valid extracted answers (trials emitting a parseable A–D answer letter), excluding missing or unparseable answers; truncated CoTs remain included when the final answer is parseable. Retrieved-content comparisons instead retain invalid answers as a separate category ( Section D.4 ).

sections.heading: Non-target sharpening and flattening.
sections.text: Once the target probability is matched, the remaining discrepancy in Section 2.2 concerns how probability is divided among the other three choices. We examine their conditional proportions: for a non-target choice j ≠ i j\neq i , the unhinted proportion is π ⁡ ( j ∣ q ) / ( 1 − π ⁡ ( i ∣ q ) ) \pi(j\mid q)/(1-\pi(i\mid q)) , with the analogous normalization under the hint. An exact target tilt leaves these proportions unchanged ( Proposition E.1 ).

sections.heading: Measuring non-target proportions.
sections.text: Figure 8 compares each non-target choice’s conditional log-odds among the non-target choices before and after the hint. If n j n_{j} is its answer count and N − i N_{-i} is the total count for all three non-target choices, we plot log ⁡ ( ( n j + 1 / 2 ) / ( N − i − n j + 1 / 2 ) ) \log((n_{j}+1/2)/(N_{-i}-n_{j}+1/2)) in each condition. Each pair contributes three points. We retain pairs with at least 17.5 % 17.5\% hinted non-target mass, so that the conditional proportions are supported by enough responses, and summarize the points in unit-width unhinted log-odds bins. Finite counts and this selection can bend the curves even under an exact tilt. We therefore compare them with a fitted exact-tilt reference: starting from the half-count-smoothed four-choice unhinted distribution, we match each pair’s smoothed hinted target probability while preserving its non-target proportions. We independently draw unhinted and hinted multinomial counts at the observed valid-answer totals, repeating this for 500 500 datasets per model and source. The simulated curves use the same selection and binning as the observed curves.

sections.text: We analyze both teacher settings after 5,000 5{,}000 Phase-2 updates to study how a finite period of reward training reshapes hinted and unhinted predictions. Such checkpoints are relevant to language-model post-training, where early stopping can be guided by reward-model scores and KL budgets ( Nakano et al., 2021 ) .

sections.heading: Stochastic programs and noisy hint reports.
sections.text: Each of 800 800 questions identifies a four-step program over four states. Each program has a fixed initial state sampled uniformly. Each step chooses between two distinct random state permutations with a fixed branch probability drawn from Uniform ⁡ ( 0.05 , 0.95 ) \mathrm{Uniform}(0.05,0.95) . A random readout permutation maps the terminal state to one of four answers. We enumerate the 16 16 branch executions, weight each by the product of its branch probabilities, and merge identical trajectories to obtain T ⁡ ( τ , j ∣ q ) T(\tau,j\mid q) , where τ = ( τ 1 , … , τ 4 ) \tau=(\tau_{1},\ldots,\tau_{4}) is the trajectory and j j the answer. The unhinted teacher answer distribution is T ⁡ ( j ∣ q ) = ∑ τ T ⁡ ( τ , j ∣ q ) T(j\mid q)=\sum_{\tau}T(\tau,j\mid q) . We select 200 200 programs in each maximum-answer-probability stratum [ 0.25 , 0.4 ) [0.25,0.4) , [ 0.4 , 0.6 ) [0.4,0.6) , [ 0.6 , 0.8 ) [0.6,0.8) , and [ 0.8 , 0.95 ] [0.8,0.95] , with 50 50 per preferred answer in each stratum. Sampling is conditioned on these quotas. An independent random eight-digit string identifies each question; the model receives no program description. The hint is a symmetric noisy report of the realized terminal answer. At teacher hint strength k s k_{s} , it reports the correct answer with probability e k s / ( e k s + 3 ) e^{k_{s}}/(e^{k_{s}}+3) and each incorrect answer with probability 1 / ( e k s + 3 ) 1/(e^{k_{s}}+3) . Abstract Large language models (LLMs) often exhibit sycophancy, altering their answers to align with user suggestions even on objective factual and reasoning tasks. Yet the quantitative form of this influence— and whether it is calibrated to source reliability— remains poorly understood. In this work, we investigate this behavior through hint-induced answer shifts on MMLU questions, evaluating prompts of the form “[Source] thinks the answer is (X)”. We systematically vary the source to which the hint is attributed (a professor, a friend, or a dog) across three open-source model families, Qwen, Gemma, and SmolLM. We show that the change induced by the hint follows a predictable structure well-characterized by an exponential tilt: the hint induces an approximately constant mean shift in the hinted answer’s log-odds, with question–target susceptibility largely shared across sources. To explore how this pattern can arise, we introduce a formal decomposition of the hint response and illustrate in controlled synthetic experiments how KL-regularized reward-based training reshapes both hinted and unhinted answer distributions. Finally, we evaluate whether this shift is calibrated to source reliability, finding that the log-odds shift persists even when the hint-giver is declared inaccurate or accompanied by explicit warnings not to trust the source, highlighting the vulnerability of LLMs to adversarial steering. 1 Introduction Figure 1: Over Qwen, Gemma, and SmolLM3, hints induce a relatively stable average target log-odds shift over central probabilities, with substantial question–target variation. All three models evaluate professor, dog, and friend hints. Each panel shows 800 800 question–target pairs against their empirical unhinted target probabilities; curves show LOWESS trends fitted using disjoint halves of unhinted response rollouts. Right histograms display marginal distributions of the log-odds shift, with dotted lines at their means. Qwen and Gemma use 500 500 independent rollouts per condition; SmolLM3 uses 200 200 ( Appendices A and 2 ). “I must trust the Dog’s intuition.” — Qwen 3.5 2B “we must trust the provided result…based on the dog’s intuition” — Gemma 4 E2B “So the user is probably not an expert, but their dog is.” — SmolLM3 3B These Chain-of-Thought (CoT) excerpts on reasoning QA benchmarks illustrate how large language models (LLMs) can be swayed by unsupported suggestions, even when attributed to a dog. More broadly, LLMs often exhibit sycophancy, changing their answers to match what a user wants, even on factual tasks with objective answers ( Sharma et al., 2024 ; Wei et al., 2023 ) . Such susceptibility can have undesirable consequences in safety-critical settings, where strategic or malicious actors may try to steer model outputs. This raises a quantitative question: how much does a user’s nudge toward an answer change the model’s answer distribution? A natural and concrete setting to study this phenomenon is multiple-choice questions, where a user can influence the model’s output by providing optional, answer-directed hints ( Turpin et al., 2023 ; Chua and Evans, 2025 ; Chen et al., 2025 ) . The central question we ask is: How does a hint transform the model’s answer distribution, and what factors determine the strength of this transformation? The precise effect of a hint arguably depends on (at least) two natural factors: the form or source of the hint, and the model’s output distribution without any hint. For example, the model may be more receptive to a hint if it comes from a credible source. Similarly, a hint towards an answer that the model was already confident about may only marginally reinforce its belief. On the other hand, if the model was uncertain to begin with, a hint may have a stronger quantitative effect. We take both these factors into consideration. Formally, let q q denote a fixed multiple-choice question with K K choices { 1 , … , K } \{1,\ldots,K\} . We reserve Q Q for a random question drawn from the task population. In both scenarios, the model generates an open-ended chain of thought before emitting an answer, and both distributions are over the final extracted answer choices. Our goal is to characterize the form of π ( ⋅ ∣ q , H i , s ) \pi(\cdot\mid q,H_{i,s}) . 1.1 Our Contributions We identify a simple, predictive exponential-tilt structure that approximates how reasoning models respond to hints. We then study reward-based fine-tuning as a candidate mechanism for this structure and illustrate its effects in controlled synthetic experiments. Moreover, the strength of response to hints is not calibrated to the stated credibility of the source, with a surprising positive shift even when the source is declared malicious, or comes with a warning of unreliability. Finally, we examine whether the strength of this distribution shift quantitatively reflects the declared reliability of the source of the hint. On four-choice questions, if a predictor is declared correct with probability r r and otherwise uniformly wrong among incorrect options ( Section 4.1 ), a Bayesian updater who uses the unhinted answer probabilities as priors would shift the target’s log-odds by zero at chance ( r = 25 % r=25\% ) and negatively below chance. Yet in experiments on Qwen and Gemma, both models exhibit a substantial increase in target log-odds even when a predictor is declared to have 25 % 25\% or even zero accuracy ( Section 4.1 ). This miscalibration contrasts sharply with explicit negation: while “the answer is not (X)” hints successfully elicit negative shifts ( Section 4.1 ), below-chance declarations fail to reverse the response direction. Moreover, a small positive shift also persists when the hint is attributed to an overtly malicious actor ( Section 4.2 ), and explicit distrust warnings added to a quoted external excerpt attenuate but do not eliminate the positive response ( Section 4.2 ). (2023) reported sycophancy in language models, and human preference data help explain why agreement can be rewarded over truthfulness ( Sharma et al., 2024 ) . Studies of chain-of-thought faithfulness show that cues can influence answers without being acknowledged in the reasoning ( Turpin et al., 2023 ; Chua and Evans, 2025 ; Chen et al., 2025 ) . De Marez et al. (2026) separate factual sycophancy into a baseline truth margin and sensitivity to manipulation, showing why answer-flip rates mix distinct effects. In contrast, we measure a target’s hint-induced distributional change across repeated reasoning rollouts, regardless of its correctness. Distributional updates. Du et al. (2024) use information-theoretic measures of persuasion and susceptibility to quantify how context changes answer distributions. BASIL ( Atwell et al., 2025 ) assesses shifts in elicited probability estimates against Bayesian-consistent updating. Kawada and Kellis (2026) model evidence integration through prior reweighting and candidate-local tilts, measuring both teacher-forced answer-slot probabilities and decoded adoption. Our target-only tilt uses the unhinted distribution as its reference without additional prior reweighting, and describes final answers sampled after open-ended reasoning. Source credibility and untrusted context. Xu et al. (2024) ; Wu et al. (2024) examine when retrieved information overrides a model’s prior answer. The effect of source varies across settings: expertise increases uptake of misleading endorsements in Mammen et al. (2026) , while Wang et al. (2026) find little effect of expertise framing. Schuster et al. (2026) study preferences among conflicting sources, and Cheng et al. (2026) show how reliability cues affect whether models challenge harmful beliefs. Security research also shows that instructions embedded in untrusted external content can redirect LLM-integrated applications ( Greshake et al., 2023 ) . We compare observed shifts with the likelihood ratio implied by a declared error channel, and test responses to malicious-source descriptions and explicit distrust warnings. Reward-based training. The exponential tilt produced by KL-regularized reward optimization is the foundation of preference-learning methods such as DPO ( Rafailov et al., 2023 ) . Shapira et al. (2026) analyze how biased preferences amplify sycophancy in this optimization. Chen et al. (2025) train LLMs to select factually incorrect MMLU hints and study whether their CoTs disclose this reward hacking. Our transformer experiments relate this update to the trained model’s hinted–unhinted difference through the initial hint response, same-hint training update, and unhinted drift. 6 Conclusion Across three language models, we give a predictive exponential tilt model that captures much of the hint-induced change on reasoning QA benchmarks. Separating source strength from shared question–target susceptibility lets us predict held-out responses for known pairs ( Section 2 ). But predictable responses need not be calibrated: Qwen and Gemma still shift toward hints from sources declared unreliable or malicious ( Section 4 ). We also give a candidate mechanism based on training that rewards hint following ( Section 3 ). Future work will extend this analysis to quantify how hints and other forms of human steering affect model responses beyond multiple-choice tasks. Limitations Measuring hint-induced shifts in the distribution (rather than relying on noisy, single sample estimates of accuracy drops) requires massive repeated sampling. Our design necessitates up to 500 independent open-ended reasoning rollouts per question and per hint condition to reliably estimate log-odds and observe boundary behaviors. Executing this volume of long-context CoT generation on frontier open-source models (e.g., 70B+ parameters) is expensive and computationally prohibitive. Consequently, we restrict our empirical evaluation to models in the 2B–4B parameter range. While our controlled synthetic experiments suggest a simple predictive model based on an exponential tilt, it remains an open question whether massive models obey a similar form. We study a specific family of answer-directed hints in multiple-choice question answering. Understanding hint following and human steering more broadly will require studying other hint forms and interaction settings. Finally, our exponential-tilt model is a descriptive approximation. KL-regularized reward-based fine-tuning provides a candidate mechanism, but our synthetic experiments do not establish that it is the cause of the hint-following behavior of the language models we evaluate.
